title: SPHERE: Mitigating the Loss of Spectral Plasticity in Mixture-of-Experts for Deep Reinforcement Learning
claim: Sequential training erodes a policy's ability to learn new tasks, because a collapsed update kernel ignores new directions while an isotropic one learns them.
layout: 2 panels, left example then right mechanism, vertical arrows, sphere spectra
description: The left panel, "Plasticity Loss", shows a robot learning Pick, Push, then Close in sequence, linked by downward arrows. Each task has a simulated robot-arm screenshot. The robot icon goes from neutral to sweating to crying. A smaller "Learning Directly" box below shows a calm robot learning Close alone and succeeding. The right panel, "Maintain Plasticity by Maximizing r_e(K)", is a two-column grid with a vertical arrow running ∇_f L → K∇_f L → Δf. The left column is a collapsed K. It shows a sphere of orange and blue points with Push and Pick axes only, labeled "New Task Ignored". Its update Δf is a flat ellipsoid. The right column is an isotropic K, with an added orange Close axis, labeled "New Task Learned". Its Δf is a full sphere. Rounded boxes frame the panels. Blue, orange and gray carry the meaning.
caption: Plasticity loss as loss of spectral plasticity. Left: Continual RL can fail on later tasks despite isolated learnability. Right: By Eq. (6), ∆f = −η K ∇fL; low effective rank of the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel (eNTK) restricts updates to a few directions (collapsed spectrum), while high eNTK effective rank enables diverse directions (isotropic spectrum).
abstract: In deep reinforcement learning (DRL), an agent is trained from a stream of experience. In a continual learning setting, such agents can suffer from plasticity loss: their ability to learn new skills from new experiences diminishes over training. Recently, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) networks have been reported to enable scaling laws and facilitate the learning of diverse skills. However, in continual reinforcement learning settings, their performance can degenerate as learning proceeds, indicating a loss of plasticity. To address this, building on Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) theory, we formalize the plasticity loss in MoE policies as a loss of spectral plasticity. We then derive a tractable proxy for spectral plasticity, one expressible in terms of individual expert feature matrices. Leveraging this proxy, we introduce SPHERE, a practical Parseval penalty tailored for MoE-based policies that alleviates the loss of spectral plasticity. On MetaWorld and HumanoidBench, SPHERE improves average success under continual RL by 133% and 50% over an unregularized MoE baseline, while maintaining higher spectral plasticity throughout training.
